young.html: Baruch Spinoza lived in the Netherlands about 350 years ago. He earned his living by grinding glass lenses for microscopes and telescopes, and he spent his free hours thinking about the biggest questions there are.

He wrote his book, the Ethics, like a geometry book. It has definitions, rules and numbered proofs, as if feelings and happiness could be worked out like triangles. He wanted every step to follow from the one before.

One of Spinoza's big ideas is about feelings. He said that when we understand why we feel something, the feeling has less power to push us around. Being angry and not knowing why is like being pulled on a rope. Understanding the cause is like getting a hand on the rope yourself.

young.name: gb-affects
young.cap: Spinoza built many feelings out of a few simple ones. Choose a starting feeling and what it is about.

young.html: Feelings detective. For one day, when you notice a strong feeling (happy, grumpy, worried), stop and write down: What am I feeling? What do I think caused it? Is that really the cause? At the end of the day, talk with a parent about whether understanding the cause changed the feeling.

full.html: Baruch (later Benedict) de Spinoza (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jewish merchants. In 1656, when he was 23, the leaders of Amsterdam's Portuguese Jewish congregation formally expelled him for what they called abominable heresies; the full reasons were not recorded. He lived quietly afterward, grinding lenses and corresponding with scientists and philosophers. He published his Theological-Political Treatise anonymously in 1670. The Ethics, finished years before, was printed only after his death, in 1677.

The full title is Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order. Each of its five parts begins with definitions and axioms, then proves numbered propositions, with notes (scholia) where Spinoza speaks more freely. The parts go from God, to the mind, to the emotions, to human bondage and, last, to human freedom.

full.text: By God, I mean a being absolutely infinite—that is, a substance consisting in infinite attributes, of which each expresses eternal and infinite essentiality.
full.author: Baruch Spinoza
full.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

full.html: Spinoza argues that there can be only one substance, a thing that exists in itself and depends on nothing else, and that this substance is God. Everything else exists in God, as a way or “mode” of God's being. We know two of God's infinite attributes: thought and extension (being spread out in space). In Part IV he writes “God or Nature” as one phrase. Everything follows from God's nature by necessity, as the properties of a triangle follow from what a triangle is.

This is Spinoza's view, and it was far from the usual teaching of the synagogues and churches of his day: his God does not choose, plan for purposes, or act from will as a person does. Readers have taken it in very different ways, as the “Going deeper” path explains.

Mind and body are one thing seen under two attributes: the mind is the idea of the body. Everything strives to keep going in its own being; Spinoza calls this striving (in Latin, conatus) the very essence of a thing. From it come three basic emotions: desire, pleasure and pain. All the others are built from these, the way compound shapes are built from simple ones.

full.name: gb-affects
full.cap: Spinoza's definitions of the emotions, in our own words: pleasure or pain, joined to different ideas, give love and hatred, hope and fear, and more.

full.text: Human infirmity in moderating and checking the emotions I name bondage: for, when a man is a prey to his emotions, he is not his own master, but lies at the mercy of fortune…
full.author: Baruch Spinoza
full.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

full.html: Freedom, for Spinoza, is not choosing without causes. It is acting from understanding. A passion is a confused idea; when we form a clear idea of its causes, it stops being a passion. The more we understand things as necessary, the less we are troubled by them. The highest good is knowledge of God, which brings a calm joy Spinoza calls the intellectual love of God, and “blessedness.”

full.text: If the way which I have pointed out as leading to this result seems exceedingly hard, it may nevertheless be discovered. Needs must it be hard, since it is so seldom found. How would it be possible, if salvation were ready to our hand, and could without great labour be found, that it should be by almost all men neglected? But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
full.author: Baruch Spinoza
full.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

full.title: Reading a Spinoza definition
full.q: Spinoza defines love as pleasure accompanied by the idea of an external cause. Using his pattern, how would you define hatred?
steps: Find the basic emotion: love is built on pleasure; its opposite is built on pain.
Keep the same added idea: “accompanied by the idea of an external cause.”
full.a: Hatred is pain accompanied by the idea of an external cause.

full.html: Thinking that because Spinoza denies free will he recommends giving up. His whole book is about becoming more active and less driven by passions, through understanding.

deep.html: For a century Spinoza's name was used, by Jewish and Christian writers alike, as a byword for unbelief, and many readers then and now hold that a God who is identical with Nature is not God in the religious sense. Others read him very differently: the German poet Novalis called him a “God-intoxicated man,” and in the 1780s a public quarrel in Germany over whether the dramatist Lessing had been a Spinozist made Spinoza widely read again. Leibniz visited him in 1676 and later criticized his system closely.

Spinoza answered Descartes by dissolving his two substances into one. Hegel, later on this ladder, said that to begin philosophy one must first be a Spinozist, though he went on to criticize him. Spinoza's account of the emotions, and his advice to understand their causes, has been compared with later psychology, while his arguments for the freedom to think and speak, in the Theological-Political Treatise, belong beside Milton's Areopagitica in this era.

items: Can ethics be proved like geometry? What would be gained, and what lost?
If everything has causes, in what sense can a person be free?
Does understanding a feeling change it?

questions: Spinoza ground lenses that helped people see more clearly. How is his book like a lens?
Think of a time a feeling “pushed you around.” Would understanding its cause have helped?
Spinoza says excellent things are hard and rare. What is something excellent that was hard for you to learn?
Spinoza was expelled by his community for his ideas, and kept writing. What do you think that took?
Is it possible to be free even if everything you do has a cause?
